column5: God teaches Moses' mouth
column6: God promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to speak, a direct Mosaic counterpart to 87:6's God-caused recitation.

column5: words put in a prophet's mouth
column6: YHWH puts words in the coming prophet's mouth and requires him to speak them, closely matching the commentary's active causative sense of making a messenger recite.

column5: YHWH puts words in Jeremiah's mouth
column6: The mouth-touching call scene makes prophetic speech a deposited divine word, illuminating 87:6 before the commentary turns to retention.

column5: words never depart from mouths
column6: The covenant promises that God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or his descendants' mouths, a generational form of the no-forgetting promise.

column5: write, teach, put the song in mouths
column6: Moses must write the song, teach it, and place it in Israel's mouths; it joins written preservation with learned recitation as the commentary does.

column5: the song will not be forgotten
column6: The song's continuing presence in descendants' mouths is explicitly said not to be forgotten, an unusually close scriptural analogue to 87:6.

column5: seek and read YHWH's book; none missing
column6: In the oracle's announced animal assembly, the reader is sent to YHWH's book and told none will be missing because his Spirit has gathered them; that concrete book-and-gathering image sharpens the commentary's claim that what God collects is not dropped.

column5: Hebrew q-r-ʾ / Arabic q-r-ʾ
column6: Hebrew q-r-ʾ is used for public reading of God's written Torah with explanation; its formal cognacy with the commentary's قرأ makes 87:6's recitation a textual and communal act, not only private memory.

column5: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
column6: Joshua is told that the Torah book must not depart from his mouth and must be meditated on continually, combining a book, oral repetition, and obedient retention.

column5: Moses writes all YHWH's words
column6: Moses' writing of all the spoken words supplies a Mosaic instance of divine speech becoming a durable written collection.

column5: Moses reads the covenant book aloud
column6: The written covenant is then read in the people's hearing, giving the read-and-hear sequence behind the commentary's movement from gathered words to pages.

column5: Moses completes writing Torah in a book
column6: The verse explicitly marks completion of Moses' written Torah, a close biblical comparator for 87:19's named Mosaic sheets.

column5: place the Torah book beside the ark
column6: The finished book is placed beside the ark as a witness, making physical custody part of preserving the words rather than leaving them only to memory.

column5: lost law book found and read
column6: Hilkiah finds the book of the Torah in the temple and gives it to Shaphan to read, a narrative reversal of scripture left out of use and then recovered.

column5: write spoken prophecies on a scroll
column6: YHWH orders Jeremiah to put all the words spoken against Israel and Judah on a scroll, directly joining oral revelation and a written surface.

column5: Baruch writes from Jeremiah's mouth
column6: Baruch writes the divine words from Jeremiah's mouth on a scroll, a particularly close scene of mediated recital becoming pages.

column5: royal burning of the scroll
column6: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the written columns; its deliberate loss gives a concrete contrary case to the commentary's claim that divine collection is not dropped.

column5: rewrite the burned scroll's former words
column6: After the scroll is burned, YHWH commands another scroll containing the former words, making restoration after textual loss part of the parallel.

column5: eat the scroll, then speak
column6: Ezekiel is commanded to consume the scroll before speaking to Israel, an embodied image of written revelation being internalized and reissued.

column5: write the vision so a reader can run
column6: The vision is written plainly on tablets for a reader, an explicit practical reason for fixing revelation in readable written form.

column5: bind testimony and seal Torah among disciples
column6: The prophet binds and seals testimony among disciples, coupling guarded writing to a community that carries it forward.

column5: I will not forget your word
column6: The psalmist's pledge not to forget God's word is the direct devotional counterpart to the commentary's contrast between forgetting and preserving.

column5: do not forget teaching; heart keeps commands
column6: Forgetting Torah is opposed to the heart's keeping commandments, closely matching the commentary's definition of forgetting as failure to hold what was entrusted.

column5: visible fringe as a reminder to obey
column6: The tassel is to be seen so Israel remembers and performs the commands; it gives a material tadhkira-like aid to recall.

column5: Hebrew z-k-r / Arabic dh-k-r
column6: The Sabbath command uses Hebrew z-k-r, formally cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر, for a liturgical remembering that issues in sanctification.

column5: Israel forgets God despite the bride comparison
column6: Jeremiah contrasts a bride who remembers her adornments with Israel that has forgotten God for countless days, making forgetfulness concrete as covenantal abandonment.

column5: forgotten Torah answered by divine forgetting
column6: Because the priests have forgotten God's Torah, God says he will forget their children; this directly parallels the commentary's reciprocal forgetting and judgment.

column5: God will not forget Zion
column6: The maternal comparison culminates in God's refusal to forget Zion, a personal counterpart to the unforgetting Lord and his record in the commentary.

column5: book of remembrance for those who fear the Name
column6: Those who fear YHWH are recorded in a book of remembrance before him, bringing together fear, the divine Name, remembering, and a written record as in 87:9-10 and 15-19.

column5: remember the Torah of Moses
column6: The closing command to remember Moses' Torah makes remembrance itself the mode by which a Mosaic written legacy remains operative.

column5: court sits and books are opened
column6: The heavenly court's opened books give a biblical image for the commentary's Lord whose knowledge of former generations is securely recorded.

column5: everlasting life and everlasting contempt
column6: Daniel's resurrection contrast gives a Hebrew Bible counterpart to 87:16-17's preference for the present life over the enduring future.

column5: grass withers but God's word stands forever
column6: The contrast between perishing grass and the enduring divine word relates the commentary's passing worldly life to retained and lasting revelation.

column5: each person dies for his own sin
column6: The legal rule rejects transferring a parent's or child's guilt, directly paralleling the commentary's cited content of Abrahamic and Mosaic sheets that no bearer carries another's burden.

column5: the sinner bears his own iniquity
column6: Ezekiel's sustained individual-accountability claim is a close theological counterpart to the commentary's 53:38 reading of the earlier sheets.

column5: spirit returns to God who gave it
column6: The return of the spirit to its giver gives a Hebrew Bible formulation beside the commentary's statement that the final endpoint is the Lord.

column5: plastered cistern that loses not a drop
column6: The rabbinic praise of learned retention as a cistern that loses no drop closely realizes the commentary's memory-as-container and dropped-object imagery.

column5: forgetting a word of learning
column6: The mishnah treats losing even one learned word as grave, making the commentary's forgetting of an entrusted teaching a concrete Torah-study ethic.

column5: Moses received and transmitted Torah
column6: Its chain from Moses through successive teachers supplies a Jewish model for the commentary's source label on transmitting a report received from another.

column5: Torah given scroll by scroll or as one whole
column6: The rabbinic dispute over separate scrolls versus a completed Torah directly frames the commentary's progression from written sheets to a gathered codex as a question about revelation's material form.

column5: Abraham fulfilled Torah before Sinai
column6: By reading Genesis 26:5 as Abraham's observance of the whole Torah before its giving to Moses, the tradition supplies a Jewish bridge to 87:19's Abraham-and-Moses pairing.

column5: burned law leaves knowledge inaccessible
column6: Ezra laments that the law has been burned and therefore the past and future cannot be known, a direct apocalypse-era opposite to a protected, retained scripture.

column5: inspired understanding and retained memory
column6: After drinking the fiery cup, Ezra's wisdom increases and his spirit retains memory, closely matching divine enablement to remember revelation.

column5: Ezra dictates while five scribes write
column6: Five men write what Ezra dictates over forty days, a detailed Jewish scene of inspired speech being gathered into text.

column5: ninety-four books written
column6: The completed production of ninety-four books makes collected written revelation, rather than a single remembered saying, the explicit outcome.

column5: Nehemiah founds a library and collects books
column6: The account of Nehemiah gathering books about kings, prophets, David, and royal letters gives a rare explicit Jewish image of assembling scattered scriptural materials.

column5: Judas collects books scattered by war
column6: Judas' recovery of books dispersed through war closely matches the commentary's path from loss and dispersal to gathered pages.

column5: books of the law torn and burned
column6: The persecution's tearing and burning of Torah books provides a historical contrary case to the durable custody imagined by 87:18-19.

column5: book of commandments held fast for life
column6: The text calls the law an enduring book and contrasts holding it fast with forsaking it, directly echoing the commentary's held versus lost revelation.

column5: Mosaic law called the covenant book
column6: Ben Sira identifies the law commanded by Moses as the book of the Most High's covenant, a Second Temple way of naming a Mosaic written corpus.

column5: this world as corridor before the world to come
column6: The corridor-and-banquet-hall contrast gives a compact rabbinic analogue to preferring the nearer worldly life over the lasting life to come.

column5: the Father's Spirit speaks through disciples
column6: Jesus assures messengers that the Spirit of their Father speaks through them, a New Testament form of divinely enabled prophetic speech.

column5: Spirit teaches and reminds disciples
column6: The Paraclete will teach all things and bring Jesus' words back to memory, directly pairing instruction with divinely secured recollection.

column5: guard the good deposit
column6: The entrusted teaching is to be guarded through the Holy Spirit, a close Christian analogue to the commentary's definition of forgetting as failing to hold an entrusted thing.

column5: God does not forget faithful work
column6: God's refusal to forget service makes divine non-forgetting an ethical and judicial claim beside the commentary's Lord who neither strays nor forgets.

column5: remember what was received and heard; keep it
column6: The church is commanded to remember received and heard teaching and to keep it, closely mapping receipt, recall, and retention onto 87:6 and 87:9.

column5: forgetful hearer after looking
column6: James' hearer immediately forgets after seeing himself, a specific Christian image of received perception that is not retained or acted on.

column5: remember prophets' words and apostolic command
column6: The letter explicitly asks readers to recall former prophetic speech and the apostolic command, joining old writings and present exhortation.

column5: provision for recall after the speaker's departure
column6: The author seeks to ensure that readers can recall the teaching after his death, making durable remembrance a stated literary purpose.

column5: do this in remembrance of me
column6: The meal command turns remembrance into a repeated communal act, a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's reminder as an instrument of recall.

column5: what was received is delivered onward
column6: Paul's received-and-delivered formula is a precise early Christian transmission chain for the commentary's sense of passing on a report from another.

column5: heard teaching entrusted through further teachers
column6: What Timothy heard is entrusted to reliable people who will teach others, making preservation a multi-generation oral chain.

column5: hold traditions taught by word or letter
column6: The command explicitly joins oral teaching and written letter as forms of retained tradition, directly comparable to recitation becoming pages.

column5: eyewitnesses deliver the word onward
column6: Luke begins from traditions delivered by eyewitnesses and servants of the word, a narrative account of report transmission before the written Gospel.

column5: word dwelling richly through teaching and admonition
column6: The indwelling word produces reciprocal teaching and admonition, a communal version of 87:9's beneficial reminder.

column5: public reading, exhortation, and teaching
column6: The triad makes public reading serve exhortation and teaching, placing Christian practice beside the commentary's joined recitation and reminder.

column5: reader, hearers, and keepers of written prophecy
column6: Blessing attaches to the reader, hearers, and those who keep a written prophecy's words, tightly joining book, recitation, hearing, and retention.

column5: taking away words from prophecy's book
column6: The warning against taking away words from the prophetic book gives a Christian textual counterpart to the commentary's insistence that what God gathers is not lost.

column5: Christ's letter written on hearts
column6: Paul contrasts ink and stone with the Spirit's writing on human hearts, a Christian reworking of the commentary's relation between held memory and written sheets.

column5: laws put in minds and written on hearts
column6: The new-covenant citation makes divine law both mentally placed and internally written, closely paralleling the commentary's movement from memory to inscription.

column5: take and eat the little scroll
column6: John consumes the revealed scroll, a New Testament image of a written message entering the prophet before further speech.

column5: must prophesy again after the scroll
column6: After the consumed scroll, John is told to prophesy again to peoples and kings; the sequence echoes internalized text becoming renewed proclamation.

column5: books and especially parchments
column6: Paul's request for books and parchments gives a concrete Christian reference for the commentary's material sheets of skin or parchment.

column5: each person bears his own load
column6: Paul's individual load supplies a direct New Testament comparator to the commentary's cited earlier-sheet claim that no bearer bears another's burden.

column5: each receives wages according to personal labor
column6: Paul's reward according to one's own labor closely parallels the commentary's cited content that a person has only what he has striven for.

column5: each receives what was done in the body
column6: Universal appearance before Christ's judgment seat gives the individual recompense setting behind the commentary's sheets-of-Moses-and-Abraham ethics.

column5: gain the world and forfeit one's life
column6: Jesus' question about gaining the whole world at the cost of life is a pointed Christian analogue to preferring worldly life over what lasts.

column5: seen things temporary; unseen things eternal
column6: The visible-temporary versus invisible-eternal contrast states the same valuation pattern developed around 87:16-17.

column5: Moses values future reward above Egypt's wealth
column6: Moses judges reproach for the Messiah greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to reward, a particularly apt Mosaic comparison for 87:16-19.

column5: the world passes; God's doer abides forever
column6: The world and its desire pass away while the doer of God's will remains forever, directly matching the contrast of worldly preference and endurance.

column5: dead judged from opened books
column6: The opened books of judgment make a Christian image of divine record-keeping beside the commentary's unforgetting Lord and the earlier sheets.

column5: remember Sabbath over wine
column6: The rabbinic derivation of Sabbath remembrance over wine interprets the Hebrew cognate z-k-r as enacted recall, sharpening the liturgical side of the commentary's ذ ك ر.

column5: letters read and exchanged between churches
column6: A letter is read in one church and exchanged for reading in another, a concrete case of written teaching being circulated rather than left as an isolated page.

column5: former writings written for present instruction
column6: Paul presents earlier written scripture as instruction for later readers, a Christian account of how first writings remain active in a new community.

column5: Scripture proclaims good news beforehand to Abraham
column6: Paul reads the Abrahamic promise as Scripture's advance proclamation of the gospel; it supplies a Christian interpretive analogue, rather than literal Abrahamic pages, for ancient Abrahamic revelation.

column5: Abrahamic covenant temporally distinguished from later law
column6: Paul's argument separates the Abrahamic promise from the law arriving 430 years later, a different ordering of Abraham and Moses that must remain visible beside 87:18-19's paired sheets.

column5: Moses wrote of Jesus
column6: Jesus' claim that Moses wrote about him is a Christian rereading of Mosaic writing that changes what a reader finds in the pages named in 87:19.

column5: sealed book cannot be read
column6: Isaiah's learned reader cannot read the sealed book, a precise inverse scene to 87:6's divine promise to make the messenger recite and retain.

column5: Abraham obeys commands, statutes, and laws
column6: Genesis presents Abraham as obedient to divine laws but does not narrate a written Abrahamic corpus; the distinction cautions against simply identifying 87:19's sheets with a Genesis document.

column5: fields and palaces of memory
column6: Augustine's image of memory as a vast interior storehouse gives a Christian interpretive companion to the commentary's container imagery for what is held, retrieved, or dropped.
